age6_8.summary: The instructions inside your body that say how to build you.
age6_8.body:
Inside almost every part of your body there are tiny instructions. They are called DNA [1].

DNA says what colour your eyes will be, and how tall you might grow.

DNA is shaped like a twisted ladder [2].

The rungs of the ladder are made of just four things. Scientists call them A, C, G and T [1].

Those four letters, in different orders, can spell out how to build a person, or a tree, or a fish.

You got half your DNA from each of your parents. That is why you look a bit like them.

age9_12.summary: The molecule that stores genetic information, and how its shape lets it copy itself.
age9_12.body:
DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is the molecule that carries the instructions for building and running living things [1].

## The four letters

DNA is a long chain built from four chemical units called bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T).

The order of these letters is the information. A stretch of DNA that spells out instructions for one job is called a gene [1].

## The double helix

DNA is not a single strand. It is two strands wound around each other in a shape called a double helix [2].

The two strands are held together by the bases pairing up, and the pairing follows a strict rule:

- **A** always pairs with **T**
- **C** always pairs with **G** [1]

## Why that rule matters

Because of the pairing rule, each strand contains all the information needed to rebuild the other one.

If you unzip the helix, each half can be used as a template to build a new partner strand. That is how DNA copies itself before a cell divides [2].

When Watson and Crick published the structure in 1953, they noted that the pairing immediately suggested a copying mechanism. Working out the shape effectively revealed how heredity works [2].

## Your DNA

A human has about 3.1 billion base pairs, packaged into 46 chromosomes [3].

Any two people share more than 99.9 percent of their DNA. Everything that makes people different is in the remaining fraction [3].

## Who found it

The structure was worked out using X-ray images made by Rosalind Franklin. A key image, known as Photo 51, was shown to Watson without Franklin's knowledge. Franklin died in 1958 and was not included in the 1962 Nobel Prize, which is not awarded after death [2].

teen.summary: The double-helical polymer encoding genetic information, whose complementary base pairing explains both faithful replication and heritable variation.
teen.body:
Deoxyribonucleic acid is the polymer that stores heritable information in all cellular life and in many viruses [1].

## Chemical structure

Each strand is a backbone of alternating deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups, with one of four nitrogenous bases attached to each sugar: the purines adenine and guanine, and the pyrimidines cytosine and thymine [1].

Two strands associate in an antiparallel double helix, one running 5' to 3' and the other 3' to 5'. Hydrogen bonding between bases holds them together, with strict complementarity: adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, guanine with cytosine via three. The G-C pair's additional bond makes GC-rich sequences more thermally stable [1].

## Structural determination

The double-helical model was published by Watson and Crick in 1953. It depended critically on X-ray diffraction data produced by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling at King's College London [2].

The diffraction image known as Photo 51, and Franklin's unpublished measurements, were shown to Watson and Crick without her knowledge or consent. Franklin's contribution was not adequately credited at the time. She died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at 37; the 1962 Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins, and is not awarded posthumously [2].

## Replication

Complementarity means each strand specifies the other. During replication the helix unwinds and each parental strand templates a new complementary strand, so each daughter molecule retains one original strand — semiconservative replication, demonstrated experimentally by Meselson and Stahl in 1958 [1].

Watson and Crick's paper noted, with conspicuous understatement, that the pairing they had postulated immediately suggested a copying mechanism.

## From sequence to function

Genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein. Transcription produces messenger RNA; translation reads it in three-base codons, each specifying an amino acid, at the ribosome [3].

The code is redundant — most amino acids have several codons — and near-universal across life, itself strong evidence for common ancestry.

## The human genome

The human genome comprises roughly 3.1 billion base pairs across 23 chromosome pairs. Estimates of protein-coding genes have fallen substantially since the Human Genome Project, settling near 20,000 — far fewer than pre-sequencing expectations [3].

Only a small percentage of the genome codes for protein. Much of the remainder is regulatory, structural or repetitive; how much is functional remains genuinely contested and depends heavily on how "function" is defined [3].

Any two humans are more than 99.9 percent identical in sequence.

adult.summary: The double-helical polynucleotide encoding heritable information; its complementary base pairing accounts simultaneously for replication fidelity and for the variation on which selection acts.
adult.body:
Deoxyribonucleic acid is the polynucleotide in which heritable genetic information is stored in all cellular organisms and many viruses [1].

## Molecular architecture

The polymer comprises a phosphodiester backbone of alternating deoxyribose and phosphate, with a nitrogenous base esterified to each sugar. Two antiparallel strands form a right-handed double helix, the canonical B-form having approximately 10.5 base pairs per turn under physiological conditions.

Watson-Crick complementarity is enforced geometrically: purine-pyrimidine pairing maintains constant helical diameter, while pairing specificity follows from hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor arrangement. A-T pairs form two hydrogen bonds, G-C pairs three, giving GC-rich duplexes higher melting temperatures [1].

## Determination of the structure

The model was published in *Nature* in April 1953 by Watson and Crick, alongside papers from Wilkins and from Franklin and Gosling.

The determination rested on X-ray fibre diffraction performed by Franklin and Gosling. Photograph 51 and Franklin's unpublished B-form measurements — including the helical parameters and the placement of the phosphate backbone externally — were communicated to Watson and Crick without her knowledge, via Wilkins and through an unpublished MRC report [2].

Franklin's data were necessary to the result and her credit at the time was inadequate. She died in 1958; the 1962 Nobel Prize was awarded to Watson, Crick and Wilkins, the prize not being conferred posthumously. The historiography here is well documented and the encyclopaedic obligation is to state it plainly rather than to reproduce the traditional account [2].

## Replication

Semiconservative replication follows directly from complementarity and was confirmed by Meselson and Stahl in 1958 using density-gradient centrifugation of isotopically labelled DNA [1].

Replication is catalysed by DNA polymerases synthesising exclusively 5' to 3', necessitating discontinuous lagging-strand synthesis. Fidelity of approximately one error per 10^9 bases derives from polymerase selectivity, 3'-to-5' proofreading exonuclease activity, and post-replicative mismatch repair.

That error rate is not zero, and this is not a defect: replication accurate enough to preserve information but not perfectly accurate is the precondition for heritable variation and thus for evolution.

## Information flow

The central dogma describes sequential transfer from DNA to RNA to protein. Transcription generates RNA; translation decodes triplet codons at the ribosome via aminoacyl-tRNAs.

The genetic code is degenerate, with 61 sense codons specifying 20 amino acids, and its near-universality across the tree of life constitutes strong evidence for descent from a common ancestor. Reverse transcription, discovered in retroviruses, established that information flow is not unidirectional [3].

## The human genome

The reference human genome comprises approximately 3.1 billion base pairs across 22 autosome pairs and two sex chromosomes. Protein-coding gene estimates have converged near 20,000, substantially below pre-sequencing projections — a well-documented instance of a widely held quantitative expectation being falsified by data [3].

Protein-coding sequence occupies roughly 1 to 2 percent of the genome. Characterisation of the remainder is contested: estimates of the functional fraction differ by an order of magnitude depending on whether function is defined biochemically, evolutionarily by sequence conservation, or genetically by phenotypic consequence. This disagreement is definitional as much as empirical and should be presented as unresolved [3].

Sequence identity between any two individuals exceeds 99.9 percent; the great majority of human genetic variation occurs within, rather than between, conventionally defined population groups [3].
